slides.title: AI Maturity Test — Intro
slides.narration: This is a diagnostic of your company's AI maturity: 35 questions across seven dimensions — strategy, people, infrastructure, data, models, adoption, and research. Think of it as a management X-ray: it reveals where your strengths are — and where structural constraints keep AI from scaling. Ninety-five percent of AI pilots fail — not because of the technology, but because companies bolt AI on top of old processes instead of changing the operating model itself. Answer honestly, and you will get your company's maturity profile and a clear view of where to start a systemic transformation. The world has already changed: either you enter the new era with AI, or your competitors will — and leave you behind. Press 'Start the test' — and find out where you really stand.

slides.title: Why You Need an AI Strategy
slides.narration: Without a strategy, a company adopts AI in total uncertainty: it doesn't know where it's going, what resources it needs, or what result counts as success. That's exactly why AI so often turns into a set of scattered pilots that don't scale and don't change the business. Strategy removes that uncertainty. It shows reality honestly — strengths, constraints, opportunities — and builds the sequence of steps that will actually lead to results. In essence, an AI strategy is a framework that connects company goals, process metrics, data, models, and AI agents into a single picture: a set of initiatives in the right order, with a clear logic of priorities. The highest maturity is when AI is no longer an appendix to strategy, but its foundation and the central element of the business model.

slides.title: Leadership Engagement
slides.narration: Leadership engagement is not about approving slide decks or sitting in working groups. Real engagement begins when executives change the way they themselves work. People watch behavior, not words: if a top manager keeps working the old way, employees read it as a direct signal that nothing needs to change. And the reverse is true: when a leader personally uses AI in management tasks — analyzing data, preparing decisions, operating in a hybrid human-machine model — AI becomes the new norm for the whole company. The leader must become the first carrier of the new operating model and culture. Maturity here is the journey from bottom-up initiatives with no support to true leadership, where executives define the AI strategy, complete the training, and lead by personal example.

slides.title: Impact and ROI
slides.narration: The logic of measuring impact is simple: if AI doesn't improve business performance, it isn't working. The key metrics are financial impact and return on investment. AI must either increase profit or reduce the cost of processes — and ideally do both. Here's what matters: AI doesn't bring new goals. All these metrics already existed in the company — they are the leaders' own performance indicators. AI radically amplifies the ability to achieve them. When leaders start working with AI and setting new standards, these metrics turn into a new norm and a new KPI: each leader is responsible not just for a process, but for how much of it is optimized by AI and how much efficiency has grown. The highest maturity is when AI itself becomes a source of company revenue.

slides.title: AI Center of Excellence
slides.narration: If there is no governance structure for AI, there is no accountability. No one sets the task, no one demands the result, no one celebrates success or dissects mistakes. AI initiatives dissolve into corporate noise and become nobody's — which means they are doomed. Everything changes radically when an AI center of excellence appears. It is an organ of managerial power where expertise, methodology, standards, best practices, data, and models accumulate. The center of excellence turns AI from chaotic experiments into a managed asset: policies, risk management, a single dashboard of initiatives, development standards, and a security model emerge. It is this manageability that lets a company achieve results that once seemed unreachable — simply because the organization is finally capable of managing them.

slides.title: Levels of Embedding AI
slides.narration: There are three levels of embedding AI into a company. The first is AI as a tool: it lives on top of processes and helps employees do individual tasks faster, without changing the logic of operations. The second is AI as an agent inside processes: it is built into value chains and performs part of the operations itself, but the human remains the bottleneck — final decisions and control still rest with them. Here the human works as an operator of the system. The third level is AI as the company's operating system: agents run operations end to end, interact with each other, adjust their actions based on data, and ensure quality. The human becomes the architect of the system. It is the depth of embedding — not the number of tools — that defines a company's real AI maturity.

slides.title: The War for AI Talent
slides.narration: In AI transformation, it's not tools or budgets that decide the outcome — it's talent. Every modern AI system is created and developed by people, so the ability to attract and grow AI specialists becomes a critical factor of future competitiveness. The war for AI talent is one of the fiercest in the market, and it cannot be won with money alone. Strong specialists need an environment where they can grow, experiment, exchange experience, and work alongside equally strong professionals. This is a science-and-engineering culture, and it cannot be faked. Mature companies build a whole ecosystem: internal AI academies, accelerators, university partnerships. The logic is simple: the strong go where they will become even stronger. Talent creates technology — and technology creates the future of companies.

slides.title: Cross-Functional AI Teams
slides.narration: The productivity of AI teams is determined not by headcount but by how they are organized and how deeply they are embedded in the business context. The model of isolated developers doesn't work in AI transformation: a team detached from the business builds solutions nobody needs. Effectiveness emerges in cross-functional teams, where domain expertise is combined with engineering power. These specialists understand both the business process and the technical capabilities of AI — so they deliver solutions faster, with higher quality and fewer iterations. Then a multiplier kicks in: teams create agents with sets of skills, and those skills scale across the whole company. This is how AI becomes an engine for spreading expertise. The highest form is autonomous AI teams — mini centers of excellence able to develop and deploy AI on their own.

slides.title: Hybrid Intelligence Culture
slides.narration: We are entering an era where a company's competitiveness is defined not by headcount or a stack of technologies, but by the combined intelligence it can assemble and direct toward its goals. It used to be collective human intelligence: teams thinking together, arguing, making decisions. Now the model has changed: every employee gets several AI assistants that help them think faster, deeper, and more precisely. A person no longer makes decisions alone — they receive critique, alternatives, scenarios, and suggestions from AI. Their thinking becomes extended. This is the culture of hybrid intelligence. The path to it starts with overcoming fear and distrust, passes through the first success stories, and ends in a state where AI is the natural 'second brain' of every employee.

slides.title: AI Academies and Skills
slides.narration: Developing AI skills is not about one-off webinars — it's about creating an environment where learning, experimentation, and innovation become the cultural norm. People want to work where strong professionals are nearby and growth is real. That's why mature companies create corporate AI academies — internal education centers that gather best practices, templates, methodologies, standards, and breakdowns of real cases. These are not formal courses but the company's concentrated expertise: an employee gets not abstract knowledge but concrete practices drawn from real experience. Maturity shows in the system: key skills are defined per role, training is regular, testing and certification are in place. The highest point is when continuous learning to work with AI becomes part of every employee's job — not a separate initiative.

slides.title: AI as Every Employee's Assistant
slides.narration: Mature integration is a model where AI becomes a personal assistant to every employee and is present at every point where the employee — as an internal customer — interacts with the company. Every day, employees naturally work with AI: they get help, recommendations, answers, reminders, and analytics — everything that makes their work faster and easier. There is also a deeper aspect: AI as emotional and cognitive support. For many people it becomes a safe way to cope with heavy workload and mental strain — and the company should provide that opportunity while guaranteeing full confidentiality. The highest level is intelligent management: AI analyzes team performance, personalizes learning, and is embedded across the entire HR cycle, culture, and communications of the company.

slides.title: Compute Power
slides.narration: Today the battle is not only for talent but also for compute. Without it, there is no model training, no inference, no industrial-scale operation of AI processes. The key principle: for AI to truly work, it must live where the company's data, services, and business processes live. If processes run on internal servers, AI must be able to run on those servers. If services are in the cloud, AI must be available in the cloud. AI has to be embedded in the infrastructure deeply enough that any model can run in the conditions where the company's real processes operate. The maturity path leads from experiments on laptops to a hybrid architecture with CI/CD and AIOps — and on to a global distributed environment with auto-scaling.

slides.title: Infrastructure Accessibility
slides.narration: Infrastructure must be not just powerful — it must be accessible. This is one of the most critical factors of AI team productivity. If a specialist can't quickly get compute or spin up an environment, their work turns into waiting instead of creating value. Speed of access to infrastructure directly determines the speed of developing models, agents, and services. When GPUs have to be begged for, access takes weeks to configure, and deployment drowns in bureaucracy, the company is slowing down its own AI transformation. Maturity here is measured simply: how much time passes from request to a working environment. The highest point is full democratization: any specialist launches the environment they need at the push of a button, through a self-service portal, with no waiting and no approvals.

slides.title: Incidents and SLA
slides.narration: Incidents are inevitable in any system — especially where AI operates: models hallucinate, data changes, integrations break, agents make mistakes. The question is not whether failures will happen, but how quickly and how well the company handles them. The benchmark is the SLA — the service level the system is obliged to provide. The ideal is when the system closes incidents autonomously or with minimal human involvement. That is the shift from reactive support to intelligent support. Another principle matters just as much: every incident is a training example. A mature company turns failures into fuel for improving its systems — not into problems swept under the rug. The peak is predictive infrastructure that anticipates failures in advance and redistributes resources before anything breaks.

slides.title: Open Source as Strategy
slides.narration: In a mature AI company, open source is part of the strategy. It is impossible to build modern AI systems while ignoring open tools: that is where industry standards and the innovations that set the pace for the whole market are born. Balance is key here. Corporate data and the models trained on it are the company's core value, and they will never become public. But tools, methods, and engineering assets are worth opening up: this is how a company improves its own ideas and receives external intellectual capital — free and continuously. Maturity runs from a complete open-source ban and outdated technology, through corporate library lists and security policies, to the state where the company itself contributes to open projects, publishes its frameworks, and participates in the community of the strongest engineers.

slides.title: Security and AI Regulation
slides.narration: Many countries are already actively regulating AI: requirements for transparency, control, accountability, and audit are becoming the norm, and companies must meet them at the level of corporate standards. But security becomes truly critical when agents act autonomously. The principle is simple: if an agent has freedom of action, it must also have a system of constraints. Otherwise it can disrupt processes, corrupt data, or trigger a chain of errors. An agent should have exactly the permissions its tasks require, plus protective mechanisms that prevent dangerous actions and define the boundaries of what is allowed and how it may act. The maturity path runs from no policies and no audit, through formalized security and compliance, to advanced cyber defense with AI-powered anomaly detection.

slides.title: Data Governance
slides.narration: Data is the habitat of AI agents. If infrastructure is the body, data is the air agents breathe: it must be clean, safe, and accessible. Agents work inside data flows, so if data is chaotic or unavailable, the agent will make mistakes — and the company will be scaling chaos. The answer is mature Data Governance: a management system that defines what data the company has, where it is stored, what quality it is, who owns it, who can be granted access, what standards apply, and how the data is used in training and decision-making. The maturity path leads from scattered data with no owners to a system where more than 80 percent of data flows are digitized and control is automated across the whole company.

slides.title: Data Factory
slides.narration: If data is scattered across Excel files and employees' personal drives, no AI agent can work reliably: it is forced to live in a chaos of incompatible formats and inconsistent data. The answer is the Data Factory. It is not necessarily a single product: it can be a classic data warehouse, a data mesh, or a hybrid model. What matters is not the approach but the principle: there is a single point of entry where data is accessible, structured, cataloged, and interconnected. An agent doesn't need to hunt for data across the company — it goes to one place and gets access to every source it is authorized to use. This sharply reduces integration complexity and speeds up decision-making. The highest maturity is when all IT systems and AI models are connected to the Data Factory.

slides.title: Data Quality
slides.narration: A simple rule applies here: bad data in — bad results out. AI agents, managers, and analysts all rely on data, and if the data is corrupted, the company makes decisions based on a false picture of the world. That is why a mature organization builds a system where quality is controlled continuously: data is checked for format compliance, absence of anomalies, correctness of values, completeness, and consistency. It is important to understand that data quality is not a one-time task or a project — it is a permanent process. The maturity path runs from a state where errors and gaps are the norm, through manual checks and validation scripts, to a unified system where checks are built into pipelines, alerts react to deviations, and anomalies are detected and corrected automatically.

slides.title: Data in Decision-Making
slides.narration: When data is used only in reports on request, the company lives in reactive management mode: it responds to events after the fact but doesn't see the future. Even regular analytics merely describes the past. The real shift happens when decisions stop being based on gut feeling and start going through a cycle of testing, validation, and forecasting: the company understands not only what happened, but also what may happen — and which actions will produce the best result. The highest point of maturity is intelligent decisions: AI helps make them in real time. It analyzes data faster than any human, sees hidden patterns, runs stress tests, and calculates 'what if' scenarios, giving leaders a fundamentally deeper understanding of the situation.

slides.title: Training Datasets
slides.narration: At the start, a company has no datasets for training models: every attempt turns into a long manual search for sources followed by labeling. Datasets are prepared for one specific pilot, without standardization — impossible to reuse or scale. In such an environment, AI forever remains an experiment. Mature companies act differently: they build datasets, describe metadata, establish labeling standards, and use data lakes for experiments. Data preparation becomes a reproducible process; automated cleaning and synthetic data appear. The highest stage is an end-to-end data loop for AI: the Data Factory is directly connected to AI pipelines, and models update automatically as the environment changes. This is what separates a company that trains models from a company that merely runs experiments.

slides.title: Model Portfolio and Registry
slides.narration: When a company enters systemic AI transformation, models stop being experiments and become a portfolio of assets that must be maintained, developed, and evaluated as seriously as any strategic resource of the business. All models should live in a single registry: which models exist, in what version, what data they were trained on, what metrics they showed at launch and show now, where exactly they are embedded in processes, and what economic effect they deliver. Versioning is especially important: the same model in different versions can produce completely different results — one version works perfectly, another degrades as the data changes. The highest maturity is when the model portfolio is managed like an investment portfolio, based on the return on investment of each model.

slides.title: Models in Production
slides.narration: It only makes sense to talk about models when they run in production. Everything else is experiments. Pilots can look impressive, but if a model isn't embedded in a working process, it changes nothing in the business: it is knowledge without action. Companies stuck at the level of endless pilots aren't really adopting AI — they are researching it. True maturity is defined by the share of models that live in production and deliver measurable impact. When a model reaches production, it becomes part of the company's operating system: it makes real decisions, affects real processes, and runs under real workloads. The highest point is when every model goes through the full MLOps cycle.

slides.title: Model Delivery Speed
slides.narration: Training a model is always an experiment: you take data, train or fine-tune a model, and check the metrics. The result is rarely perfect on the first attempt, which is why the process is iterative and demands flexibility and speed. The speed at which a company can train, retrain, and ship models to production becomes a critical factor of competitiveness. If the environment changes daily and market conditions are unstable, the company must adapt at the same pace. In a world where AI has become the foundation of business processes, this means one thing: the model delivery cycle must be as short as possible. The maturity path runs from quarters per model, through standardized processes and templates, to continuous release — when training and deployment take hours, not months.

slides.title: Model Monitoring
slides.narration: Every model degrades over time: data changes, context shifts, user behavior evolves. Without monitoring, this degradation goes unnoticed, and the model's decisions become less and less accurate — and more and more dangerous for the business. At early maturity levels, a deployed model lives on its own until something breaks, and analysts check its quality after the fact. Next, the company starts tracking basic metrics of drift, quality, and stability. High maturity means automated monitoring: an MLOps loop controls the models, and anomalies are handled centrally. The peak is intelligent control, when monitoring is performed by AI agents themselves: they predict degradation in advance and assess its impact on business outcomes.

slides.title: MLOps and Engineering Culture
slides.narration: What matters here is not only the technology but the culture of engineering work — it determines whether solutions are robust, maintainable, and able to live long in production. In a mature company, development, testing, deployment, monitoring, and retraining of models form a single production cycle: no manual actions, no chaotic releases — only standardized pipelines, automated checks, and reproducible results. Every model goes through A/B testing and has documentation. The main goal is to make solutions maintainable, so a model can be updated safely and the company doesn't depend on one irreplaceable person, but stands on a mature engineering culture. The maturity path leads from handcrafted research scripts to MLOps as an architectural norm, where every ML development process is automated.

slides.title: AI Process Coverage
slides.narration: The key maturity question is not how many models were built or pilots run, but what share of real business processes already operates with AI involved — or under AI control. A process is a chain of concrete operations: collecting and passing data, making decisions, checking conditions, executing actions. And AI can cover different depths: in some places it merely assists an employee, in others it automates individual operations, and in others it runs the process entirely. That's why measurement must be precise: what part of the process is automated, and how many operations run without human involvement. A practical tip: decompose processes down to individual operations — it makes it much easier to see what exactly to automate. The highest maturity is autonomous execution, when AI runs most of the everyday RUN processes.

slides.title: Augmentation: AI Amplifies People
slides.narration: AI transformation is not only about automation. In some processes the human is irreplaceable: in management, creativity, strategic decisions, complex communication. There, AI doesn't displace the human — it amplifies them. That is augmentation: AI gives a person new capabilities and a new level of thinking. It's important to understand: a mature company is not one where everything is automated. It is one where humans and AI work in symbiosis, in a hybrid model where every business function gets a co-pilot. The leader remains the human who makes the decision — but now makes it together with AI, drawing on analysis, scenarios, and forecasts. The highest form is the 'human plus agent' symbiosis: AI performs a significant share of operations, while the human sets goals and meaning.

slides.title: AI in Customer Journeys
slides.narration: Customer journey coverage shows how deeply AI is embedded in the customer's interaction with the company — from first contact to the end of service. It is one of the most vivid indicators of organizational maturity. Customers should see, feel, and receive value from AI at every stage where it is appropriate: AI personalizes offers, selects optimal products, and recognizes the customer's needs before they have even articulated them. At the same time, it behaves predictably, is never toxic, and stays accountable within established rules. But the principle cuts both ways: humans remain where humans are needed — where empathy, emotional engagement, and complex problem-solving are required. The highest maturity is a complete intelligent loop, where an AI agent accompanies the customer along an entirely personalized journey.

slides.title: AI Implementation Framework
slides.narration: Without a unified implementation framework, AI projects turn into chaos: every department does its own thing, timelines are impossible to predict, quality fluctuates, and teams constantly don't know what to do next. When a framework appears, the situation changes radically: it lays down rails and turns AI adoption from exploratory wandering into a production process, where every stage has its artifacts, its logic, and its expected results. The framework sets the standards: how data is collected, how a model is selected, how deployment and monitoring are done. The maturity path runs from handcrafted projects with no methodology, through standardization and A/B testing, to delivery through an AI center of excellence — and finally to an autonomous cycle where the whole journey runs through an end-to-end AgentOps loop.

slides.title: User Adoption of AI
slides.narration: The end user of any AI rollout is a specific person who works with the tool every day. If that person doesn't understand how to use the agent, doesn't trust it, or feels the tool gets in the way — the rollout has failed, however sophisticated the technology. Success is when people genuinely use the tool, get value from it, and it becomes a natural part of their workflows. That's why the usage metric is the key indicator. The environment matters too: agents must be embedded in the digital space employees already inhabit. If the company lives in messengers, the agent should appear there — as one more new colleague. The highest maturity is full symbiosis: AI is perceived as a digital colleague, and trust and satisfaction exceed 90 percent.

slides.title: Academic Partnerships
slides.narration: A company that doesn't do research and doesn't work with academic partners is doomed to use yesterday's technologies — while its competitors are already creating tomorrow's. A modern AI company must be deeply embedded in the scientific environment. Universities and laboratories are the source of the latest technology: new architectures, optimization methods, training approaches, and new types of models are born there. So are the talents capable of solving non-standard problems. A mature company doesn't hide knowledge: it publishes papers, shares results, speaks at conferences, and runs its own scientific seminars. The maturity path leads from no contact with academia, through one-off projects, to stable scientific alliances, joint R&D programs, and a full-fledged innovation ecosystem.

slides.title: R&D as an Experiment Factory
slides.narration: Modern AI R&D is a factory of scientific experiments inside the business. The more research iterations a company runs, the higher the probability of a breakthrough. In a mature organization, research is integrated into product work yet follows the scientific method: hypothesis, experiment design, data collection, testing, recorded results, and conclusions for the next iterations. AI itself plays the key role here: it accelerates the entire research cycle and becomes a participant in R&D rather than just a tool. It analyzes new publications, proposes ideas, refines hypotheses, designs sets of experiments, tests options, and points to directions a human might never notice. The highest maturity is continuous research embedded directly into the company's operating model.

slides.title: Research Share in the Portfolio
slides.narration: The more routine work a company hands over to AI, the more resources it frees up for research — and that is the moment it starts moving into the class of true technology leaders. In a mature company, research is a full-fledged part of the project portfolio. The benchmark is simple: if at least one project in ten is a research project, that is a sign of high maturity. The company can hold the balance between running today's processes and creating the future. Research initiatives let the company look beyond its current horizon of possibilities, try new methods, and test non-trivial ideas. The maturity path runs from no R&D and lone enthusiasts to a balanced portfolio — and to research as a strategic block that pushes the whole industry forward.

slides.title: Applicability of R&D Results
slides.narration: The key indicator of R&D maturity is applicability: the ability to turn scientific work into real technologies that operate in products, processes, and the operational loop. The formula is simple: research for the sake of research is academic activity; research for the sake of practice is technological progress. A mature company uses R&D exactly this way: universities and research centers help explore new methods, joint laboratories solve the company's specific problems, a scientific publication goes out to academia — while inside the company remains a technology that can be built into products, processes, and AI agents. The highest maturity is a complete innovation loop, where every significant R&D result influences the strategy and the economics of the business.

slides.title: Community Activity
slides.narration: Activity in professional communities is not about PR or beautiful keynotes. It shows how much a company genuinely influences the development of its industry and sets the direction for the whole market. A mature organization doesn't close in on itself: it shares knowledge, publishes research results, talks about new methods, and speaks at scientific and industry conferences. This is a sign of strength, not weakness — such companies are confident because they know they can create even more. When a company demonstrates its technology and shares its work, it becomes a reference point for others: that is how the industry's technological standards are formed. The maturity path runs from complete non-publicity, through occasional talks, to thought leadership — and finally to setting the standard for the industry.
